Jessica Jones

Poet · Educator · Writer of Place

Lecturer, Kent State University at Stark campus

Jessica Jones writes poems and makes photographs rooted in particular places: Northern Appalachia, where she grew up with strong ties to the land; rural Montana; and the places her travels have taken her.

Her work traces layered local history, the human cost of copper and silver mining, environmental sustainability and land-based culture. She also writes ekphrastic poems in response to photographs of city walls, murals and graffiti.

She is a Lecturer at the Kent State University at Stark campus, where she teaches creative writing, place-based composition, Native literature, travel writing and poetry.

A sense of place is integral to my work as a writer and artist.

Jessica Jones

Featured poems

Ghost Flight, Berkeley Pit

Butte, Montana

You can’t see the copper, says our guide,
You’ll see some sparkles—but that’s fool’s gold.
Moly’s in your mascara and Ensure breakfast drink,
       but it’s mostly in hard steel that goes to PA.
This mine’s the second largest consumer of electricity in the state of Montana.
            Those 600 ton trucks? They don’t go to the garage to get fixed,
            You gotta fix ’em yourself on the field in January.
            Work here long enough you’ll be defined by the dimensions of the pit.

Through the windows of his van, we study its cavernous gap:
One mile long, half a mile wide, 900 feet deep and acidic—
slowly eating deeper into the earth each year.
Heavy with cadmium, arsenic, cobalt. Unearthly green.

Nov 28, 2016, snow geese came down outta Yukon, Alaska.
It was warm up there so they skipped their Canadian stops aimin’ for Texas,
but the weather changed, and everything froze.
No open water in Great Falls.
Helena was ice.
Missoula doesn’t have a lake.
Berkeley was the last fluid surface.
We started getting calls from Anaconda
that the sky was filled with geese.
Sounded like helicopters overhead.
I mean— it was white with snow geese.
Estimated 80-100,000 birds on radar.
We surrounded ’em with high power air rifles, drones…
              It was minus 20 degrees Fahrenheit
             an’ our guys were shootin’ rounds at 3AM.

Day two, we knew this was gonna be a mortality situation.
Tried to get a flotilla device down there, called the news stations.
Day three, four, we’re seein’ corpses:
                A snow goose has no kidney, so they drink water to feel better.
                The wildlife biologists say it’s like humans drinking ocean water…
                            About 800 of ’em washed toward the station,
                           blisters up and down their bowels.
Every major newspaper in the country was calling me.
And just ordinary people thinking they had the solution—
                like we hadn’t tried everything over the years.
A lady from Atlanta said to poke a hole in the pit,
               let water run to California.
Other people said build a dome,
well that dome would have to be the size of 10 Dallas Cowboy stadiums.
I got death threats
            – I mean—
            I was in 10th grade when they turned off the pumps for Berkely Pit!
Some Iowa farmer called to say ‘good job’
                and wanted to know how to run the geese off his corn fields.
                I called him back just to tell him we didn’t do it on purpose.

 We lost about 4,000.

Currently, we get 99.8 of any birds out.
There’s 6 million snow geese a year fly south.
If we see a flock comin’, it’ll be 3rd of July here in Butte.

                  They’re vocal… you can hear ’em a mile away.
                  They got red feet an’ pink bills.
                  Their lifespan’s anywhere from 10-20 years
                                  and they mate for life.

               When they come in, it’s like—
                                 it’s like a soft white cloud,
                                 some people call it a ‘snowstorm’
                                 like confetti in the sky,
                                 black-tipped wings —

He can’t say it in a hard hat or a company truck
but when his voice falls silent his face speaks—

                 I wonder if anybody saw            their     spirits
                lifting              off—
                strong white bodies
                carrying  ’em       up,
                calling to relatives,    in     ancestral   chorus—

                    This way!
                           This
                                    way!

                                                              This

                                                                           way!

                                                                           We’re

                                                                                                          almost

                                                                                                                                                       to

                                                                                                                      ancient

                                                                                     moving                  waters

                                                          wild,                 with fish—
                                                 and reeds


                                                   lapping  at
                      blameless          dreams.

First published by Poets for Science in The Nature of Our Times, January 15, 2025

Exocoetidae

Great Lakes

Maybe mercy is the feather
that gives hope plumage—
How else would men love
in the aftermath of brotherly war?
Such questions call to me like crows—
jagged, gnawing, at 2am.
Saint Frances—
how did you conjure grace
for those that killed
soft creatures with bright eyes?
How did you shelter the dove
nested in your own breast?
The ribcage hardly feels stanza
enough to carry out its job.
What action in domestic affairs?
Unlikely flight? Exocoetidae—
like an ancient fish donning wings
to survive across eons?
Or perhaps an upheld hand—
universal sign for:
Come no closer,
Go in peace.
What in Genocide’s shadow?
Exodus? Sanctions? Arrest?
Not death for death—
at least      some courage beyond complicity—
then     years     grappling
with grief’s heavy stones.
At the bottom of the stream
beneath cloud cover, swirling mud eddies,
and hungry minnows
the water is clear, still.
There, the bones open
and the heart swims out.

First published by Poets for Science in The Nature of Our Times, January 15, 2025

Edited collection

Forthcoming

Wide Branches, Deep Roots: How Appalachian Wisdom Can Help in the Fight for a Sustainable Future

Edited by Jessica M. Jones and Amanda E. Hayes

West Virginia University Press · December 2026

To be Appalachian is to define oneself in terms of a place. Where we’re from plays a tremendous role in who we are, through storytelling about our homeplaces and the people who have loved them. However, what goes largely unaddressed is how this love of place can contribute to sustainability within the region, which has notoriously faced on-going environmental threats from extraction industries. The reality is that our relationship with the environment is thorny and intertwined with our identities, histories, and economic realities. The authors in the collection get down among the thorns to explore what sustainability means in Appalachia and how we can utilize the power of traditional folkways to achieve it.

— West Virginia University Press
Order the book
Publisher’s page

Poetry chapbook

Bitterroot

Finishing Line Press · 2018

Poems set on the Flathead Indian Reservation.

Buy Bitterroot

About the book

Traversing the sparse and sometimes rugged territory from Stevensville, Montana to the Flathead Indian Reservation, Bitterroot poignantly witnesses the complex intersections of Native and non-Native culture in Montana. A testament to the spirit of the land and those shaped by it, this collection reveals the ways in which the West remains both fraught with tension and modeled by beauty. Narrated by a young teacher with unexpected ties to the children in her classroom, each poem unfolds another layer of mountain life—from hauling wood and making fire to navigating a blizzard and grieving the loss of a student. Page by page, life presses closely against that which is raw and wild, lending individual moments a sense of urgency: “What I remember/ from Ovando, though, is stars. Stars and ice/ and the shock of our short inward breath.”

Attentive to a long tradition of tough Montana poets, Jessica Jones pays homage to giants such as Richard Hugo and James Welch while befriending contemporary writers like Jennifer Finley Greene and Robert Lee. A runner-up with Open Country Press and honorable mention with CutBank at University of Montana, Bitterroot is essential for any avid reader of Western literature.

— Finishing Line Press

Anthologies

Light Enters the Grove

Kent State University Press · 2024

An anthology about Cuyahoga Valley National Park. It also includes work by her colleague Bob King.

Buy the book →

Dear Vaccine

Kent State University Press · 2022

People from around the world reflect on the COVID-19 pandemic and vaccine through poetry

In March 2021, the Wick Poetry Center at Kent State University and the University of Arizona Poetry Center launched the website for the Global Vaccine Poem project, inviting anyone to share experiences of the pandemic and vaccination through poetry. Dear Vaccine features selections from over 2,000 poetry submissions to the project, which come from all 50 states and 118 different countries.

— Kent State University Press

Buy the book →

Bright Bones: Contemporary Montana Writing

Open Country Press · 2018

Bright Bones is an anthology of innovative literature, and is currently available at Open Country Press. The cover art is by Butte artist Kelly Packer. Bright Bones includes fresh poems, stories, lyric essays and translations, as well as cross-genre, collaborative and experimental works. Emerging and established writers from Montana and/or those who have spent a significant amount of time in Montana are featured.

— Open Country Press

Open Country Press →

Poems Across the Big Sky

Many Voices Press · 2006

Whether in Montana classrooms or in solitude, the beauty, complexity, and struggle of lives in Montana have inspired the remarkable variety of voices which comprise Poems Across the Big Sky. The poets included are female as well as male, Native American as well as non-Native, gay as well as straight, urban as well as rural. Some of them write in the Native languages of Montana, and also in English. Together they provide a portrait of Montana which challenges and prods us to a new, more inclusive and comprehensive understanding of the bittersweet essence of contemporary life in Montana Reservations, cities, small towns, isolated ranches, cabins, prairies, and mountains.

— Margaret C. Kingsland (from the Introduction)

item.content:encoded:
A sense of place is integral to my work as a writer and artist.

Short bio

Jessica Jones is a poet, photographer and college educator whose work centers on a sense of place. She comes from a long line of makers and musicians in Northern Appalachia, where she grew up with strong ties to the land, and her poems and photographs move between that region, rural Montana and her travels. She is the author of the poetry chapbook Bitterroot (Finishing Line Press, 2018) and co-editor, with Amanda E. Hayes, of Wide Branches, Deep Roots (West Virginia University Press, forthcoming December 2026). Her work appears in the anthology Light Enters the Grove (Kent State University Press, 2024). She holds an M.A. in English from the University of Montana and is a Lecturer at the Kent State University at Stark campus, where she teaches creative writing, place-based composition, Native literature, travel writing and poetry.

Long bio

Jessica Jones is a poet, photographer and college educator whose work centers on a sense of place. She comes from a long line of makers and musicians in Northern Appalachia, where she grew up with strong ties to the land, and her poems and photographs are rooted in that region, in rural Montana and in the places her travels have taken her. Her work explores layered local history, the human cost of copper and silver mining, environmental sustainability and land-based culture. She also writes ekphrastic poems that respond to photographs of city walls, murals and graffiti.

She is the author of the poetry chapbook Bitterroot (Finishing Line Press, 2018), set on the Flathead Indian Reservation. With Amanda E. Hayes, she co-edited Wide Branches, Deep Roots: How Appalachian Wisdom Can Help in the Fight for a Sustainable Future (West Virginia University Press, forthcoming December 2026), a collection exploring what sustainability means in Appalachia and how traditional folkways can help achieve it. Her poetry and essays have appeared in journals and anthologies. Her poems appear in the anthologies Light Enters the Grove (Kent State University Press, 2024), Dear Vaccine, Bright Bones and Poems Across the Big Sky, and five of her poems, including “Ghost Flight, Berkeley Pit” and “Exocoetidae,” were selected for Poets for Science.

She was Poet-in-Residence at Cuyahoga Valley National Park (2007–2008) and Writer-in-Residence at Calcutta Mercy Hospital in India. In the summer of 2024 she was writer-in-residence with the Open AIR artist residency in Philipsburg, Montana, where she led library writing workshops for adults and teens, taught art camp at the local elementary school, and created “Dear Philipsburg,” a community poem platform where residents shared memories, photos and poems.

Jones holds an M.A. in English from the University of Montana, where she studied place-based and Indigenous education, as well as K-12 teaching licensure and training in Indian Education for All. She taught middle school on the Flathead Indian Reservation for several years and teaches regularly with Upward Bound, serving students from the Blackfeet Reservation and Missoula County Public Schools. She is a Lecturer at the Kent State University at Stark campus, where she teaches creative writing, place-based composition, Native literature, travel writing and poetry.

Away from the page and the classroom, she prefers to live life out of doors. She enjoys hiking, paddle boarding, and time with loved ones and her cat, Magnolia.
